title: Appeal to Tradition Fallacy Explained
tags: pale blue thoughts appeal to tradition
description:
The Appeal to Tradition is one of the most common logical fallacies we encounter in everyday life. It argues that something must be true or good simply because “that’s how it’s always been done.” From politics to religion, from family customs to alternative medicine, this fallacy thrives wherever people resist change.

In this video, we break down the logic behind appeal to tradition and show why it fails. Just because an idea or practice is old doesn’t make it right. Racism, slavery, and sexism were “traditions” too, yet they were unjust and harmful. Today, we still see the same flawed reasoning:

Ayurveda and other pseudosciences claiming legitimacy because they’re “centuries old.”
Religious rituals defended only on the basis of age.
Festivals like Diwali crackers or idol immersions justified because “it’s always been done.”
Family expectations pushing careers or lifestyles simply because of custom.

We also contrast appeal to tradition with its opposite, the appeal to novelty, which wrongly assumes new things are always better. Both are traps that ignore evidence and reason.

If you’ve searched for appeal to tradition fallacy, logical fallacies explained, pseudoscience debunked, tradition vs science, or critical thinking tools, this video gives you the rational perspective.

Like, comment, share, and hype this video so more people can learn to question outdated traditions and embrace evidence-based reasoning.

00:00 – Intro: What is Appeal to Tradition?
01:30 – Why Tradition Feels Convincing
03:10 – Faulty Assumptions Exposed
05:00 – Examples: Medicine, Religion & Festivals
07:20 – Appeal to Tradition vs Novelty
09:10 – How to Overcome This Fallacy

comments.text:
*Oldest Religion, Sarrrrrrr!*

Just because a religion is the oldest doesn’t guarantee it’s factual or correct. For example, if 500 years from now someone were to discover an ancient atomic model theory resembling a watermelon, they couldn’t claim it’s true simply because it’s older than modern atomic theories. This is the same appeal to tradition fallacy used by pagans who believed their customs and texts were valid just because they had been followed for generations.

The flaw here is in thinking that age equals truth, without considering evidence or reasoning. The appeal to tradition ignores the need for factual support, not just antiquity. 

If you want to test the authenticity of something, like the Quran, read its message, then understand what its actually trying to achieve with x y z laws and applications, place yourself 1,400 years ago, and then compare it to the modern world then it will resonates with you.

 Its teachings transcend time, confirm previous scriptures, and provide clarity—not because it’s the oldest, but because of its universal and timeless message.

transcript: Hello and welcome to yet another video in the logical fallacy series. Thank you for a good response to the appeal to authority fallacy episode. Glad to know that many of you liked it. Today we will look at a logical fallacy which is exhibited by most of us Indians. In fact, you can say it is in our blood. Take a look at this famous dialogue from the movie Mohabbatein. Yes, today we will look at appeal to tradition. While an appeal to tradition may sound convincing, you shouldn't let it fool you. This video will help you to be in the lookout for arguments that take this form and will help you to prevent yourself from accidentally using it yourself. Welcome to Pale Blue Thoughts, the channel which promotes scientific temper and denounces pseudoscience. An appeal to tradition is a logical fallacy people use to claim that a current circumstance, process, or statement is true or superior to an alternative because it is how it's always been done. There isn't data or evidence proving that such a belief is in fact better. It is just assumed to be so because of its tradition or history of producing favorable outcomes. You will see this fallacy in action almost everywhere in politics, in religion, your home, with your parents and family, and even in the workplace. People are reluctant to change from their old set of beliefs because that is how they have done it for so long. People are set in their ways. They fear the unknown and unless the change results in a direct benefit to them, they are not motivated to make it. Let us first look at the logical form of the fallacy. X has been done for a long time, therefore X is right or good. This reasoning is fallacious because it relies on historical preferences rather than facts to prove its point. Because there is no data, there is not enough documentation to assert a claim. In fact, admitting that the only reason behind something is historical preference highlights the fact that the speaker has no supportive evidence. An appeal to tradition makes two faulty assumptions. The old way of thinking was correct because it was proven at some point. And two, any justification that was used in the past is still valid. But the truth is a tradition could have been initially been based on a false premise and even if something was true at one time, circumstances can change that revoke this truth. Take the case of Ayurveda. At one time, with the limited understanding of the human body, ancient yogis wrote some highly imaginative concepts about the human body. They believed in the humor systems of vata, pita, and kapha because they thought that there was a vital force that was present within us which drove our engines. They also thought that plants were provided for us to make food and to provide us with medicines. However, today we know that the humoral theory is false and that plants are not designed for our food and that they contain a lot of chemicals that could harm us. The plants make these poisons to ward them off from their enemies and they store their food for their own consumption and for propagating their species. This is a typical example of a tradition that is based on a false premise, the humoral theory. Today circumstances have changed and we know much more truths, but many people still like to cling on to the old belief because their logic is that it is how it has always been done and there is no need to change. All forms of alternative medicine are known for their long histories that have stood the test of time, which makes alternative medicine practitioners insist that it is more relevant than modern scientific findings. Arguments in favor of alternative are loaded with logical fallacies and the appeal to tradition is certainly one of them. Having a long tradition of use does not imply safety and efficacy. For that, you need to prove it using the much more reliable scientific methods. The appeal to tradition fallacy is very similar to the bandwagon fallacy, which is based on the assumption that the majority's opinion is automatically correct due to the number of people who believe in it. However, this logic only proves that a belief is common, not that it is accurate. One typical example that you most often see around are family traditions. Our family has a long tradition of male family members becoming chartered accountants. My great-grandfather, grandfather, and father were all chartered accountants. Thus, it is right and the only option for me to become an accountant, too. Whether I can correctly tally a balance sheet is not a criteria. Now, think of a child in the family who has dreams of pursuing a career in arts or sports. Think of his life if he's forced to choose a career which does not interest him or her. Look at another example. Gays have never had the legal right to marry. Therefore, it must be wrong and we shouldn't be legalizing gay marriages now. Again, see how detrimental is this sort of thinking is for our society if we continue to live with such a fallacy. There are few things in life that involve the level of tradition that religion does. While each religion may have its own traditions, they are all ancient and people are scared to question these traditions. People have been practicing religions for thousands of years. With this in mind, some may argue that at least some form of religion must be true because so many people have believed in religious systems for so long. This argument is an appeal to tradition because the only evidence it offers that proves the validity of the argument in favor of religion is the span of its duration. So, it may be true that people have generally believed in religion for longer than they haven't, but the conclusion that religion is true cannot be made on this observation. We would need more evidence about religion than its age before we could accept it as being either true or false, which makes this argument a logical fallacy. Also, consider how other age-old arguments have failed in the past. The claim that Earth is flat or the Earth is the center of the universe, even when almost all of the people on Earth believed that the Earth was flat or that it was stationary, the Earth was casually orbiting the sun in the oblate spheroid form. Yet another appeal to tradition happens with festivals. Some festivals like Diwali had lighting diyas as a tradition, but over time people have resorted to burning crackers and polluting the environment. That is now a tradition and people often react illogically when the government bans crackers for instance. Ganesh Chaturthi is yet another festival where idols are immersed in river bodies, which pollutes them. Even though this is common knowledge, people are not willing to change things. Bakr-Id, a festival which glorifies the story of a father attempting to kill his own son because of a dream that he saw, and to this day hundreds of thousands of goats are sacrificed every year. All examples of appeal to tradition. Very often, traditions stem from religious or archaic beliefs, and until people question the logic and reasoning behind such traditions, people who are negatively affected by such traditions will continue to suffer. Just because it was acceptable in past cultures and times doesn't mean it is acceptable today. Think racism, sexism, slavery, and you will get the idea. It is also widely used in marketing. Pickles that are just like how your grandmother used to make or curry powder that your mom used to make are a few examples. Another example is the notion that just because something is old, then it must be good. You often see it with alternate medicine systems like Ayurveda and yoga, where the only criteria people claim it is good is because it has been practiced for centuries. There is no other evidence for the benefit of the claims. The opposite of appeal to tradition fallacy is one called appeal to novelty. It occurs when someone asserts that something must be true or good because it is new. For example, if someone says that a certain product must be better than its old version solely on the basis that it is newer, they are guilty of committing an appeal to novelty. So, how can you overcome this fallacy? If someone uses this logical fallacy, then they should be presented with a contrary question. Why shouldn't something be done this way? Thus forcing them to think of the alternate option or picture a situation in which the tradition has been broken. This can help them realize that there are other ways to successfully get things accomplished. Like other fallacies, claims regarding this logical fallacy aren't necessarily untrue. The problem is when the only evidence offered is the long-standing history of an issue or phenomenon. After all, if an idea can stand the test of time, it can also be validated through retesting. So, retesting the logic or validation of an age-old claim is the right thing to do. So, make them relook at the same situation from another angle.
